subject: Biology
title: What Is an Ecosystem?
description: A quick, practical guide to What Is an Ecosystem?.

hook.text: A pond, a forest, and a coral reef look nothing alike—but they all follow the same rules.

buildup.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living environment.

discovery.text: Energy flows through ecosystems and nutrients cycle within them, connecting everything.

twist.text: Remove one species and the ripple effects can transform the entire system.

climax.text: From a tiny puddle to the Amazon rainforest, ecosystems sustain all life on Earth.

quiz.question: What two things connect all parts of an ecosystem?

details.summary: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their non-living environment as an integrated system. Energy flows through trophic levels while nutrients cycle between organisms, soil, water, and atmosphere, creating the functional units that sustain all life on Earth.
details.whyItMatters: Ecosystems provide services worth trillions of dollars annually, including clean air, water purification, pollination, and climate regulation. Understanding how ecosystems function is essential for managing the natural resources humanity depends u...
takeaways: Ecosystems include both living organisms and their non-living environment
Energy flows one way through ecosystems while nutrients cycle repeatedly
Even small ecosystems can contain thousands of interacting species

faq.question: What is the difference between an ecosystem and a biome?
faq.answer: An ecosystem is a specific community and its environment at any scale, from a pond to a forest. A biome is a large-scale category of ecosystems sharing similar climate and vegetation, like tropical rainforest or tundra, spanning entire continents.

faq.question: What are ecosystem services?
faq.answer: Services that ecosystems provide to humanity for free, including oxygen production, water filtration, flood control, pollination, carbon storage, and soil formation. These services have been valued at trillions of dollars annually and cannot be easily replaced by technology.
